_comment: A LABELED SET OF 200 REAL MEASURES that received a recorded House
roll-call vote in the 118th or 119th Congress, captured live from
api.congress.gov during story 5.5 (2026-10-19) with their real CRS policy
area and legislative subject terms.
=== WHAT THIS SET MEASURED, AND WHAT IT FOUND =======================
Story 5.5's acceptance criterion is 'at least 85% precision on a 200-bill
labeled set'. Measured against this set, the rule-based v0 classifier
scores 54.2% precision (122 of 225 proposed tags correct) under the
strict standard below, and 65.8% under a deliberately lenient one.
**The 85% bar is not met, and the classifier therefore accepts no tag
automatically** -- every tag is routed to the QA queue. See
app/ingest/bill_topic_classifier.py's docstring for the full finding and
why no threshold fixes it.
Every distinct measure voted on in House roll calls of the 118th and
119th Congresses was collected first (889 measures, from 2,480 roll-call
fetches). A random draw from those would be ~18% 'Congress' and
'Government Operations' procedural measures and would under-represent the
policy areas this product is actually about, so the set is STRATIFIED BY
CRS POLICY AREA: up to 12 measures per distinct policy area
(random.seed(42)), then the first 200 in (congress, type, number) order.
All 30 policy areas that occur on House-voted measures are represented.
Note what the population is NOT: it is not all bills. A random sample of
introduced bills is ~83% bills with ZERO CRS subject terms (measured
live), which would measure nothing. Measures that reach a recorded vote
are 100% CRS-indexed, and they are the population story 5.5 exists to
serve, because its whole purpose is to turn VOTES into stance positions.
For each tag the classifier proposed, one question was asked:
Would a voter who selected a stance under this taxonomy topic consider
this bill's recorded vote to be evidence about that stance?
Judged from the bill's own title plus its full CRS subject list -- both
public record and both stored in this fixture, so every judgment is
re-checkable by a reviewer who disagrees with it.
Labels are recorded per tag as `correct: true|false`, and every FALSE
label carries a `why_wrong` string naming the specific reason. Negative
judgments are spelled out individually and positives are the default,
deliberately: it makes each rejection reviewable on its own terms and
gives a reviewer who disagrees exactly one line to argue with.
Three judgment calls are flagged in their own `why_wrong` text as
'labeled false so the judgment is visible' -- cases a reasonable reviewer
might score the other way (a sense-of-Congress resolution against a
carbon tax; Title IX athletics bills under 'anti-discrimination
enforcement'). They are a handful of 103 and do not move the conclusion:
even scoring all of them correct leaves precision far below 85%.
CRS subject terms record what a bill MENTIONS, not what it is ABOUT, and
that gap is the whole result. Worked examples from this set:
* 'Supporting America's Children and Families Act' carries
'Correctional facilities and imprisonment' and 'Detention of persons'
-- parental incarceration as a child-welfare RISK FACTOR. Two
agreeing terms, so the corroboration rule accepted it as a sentencing
tag. It is a child-welfare bill.
* 'Billie Jean King Congressional Gold Medal Act' carries 'Sex, gender,
sexual orientation discrimination' -- the honoree's biography, not a
provision.
* 'Wounded Warrior Access Act' is filed under the 'Armed Forces and
National Security' policy area, which no mapping can distinguish from
a defense-spending bill.
None of these is a threshold that was set wrong. Each is a bill whose CRS
indexing is CORRECT and whose topic cannot be recovered from it.
